findings.source_passage: Hugo died in agonies of remorse and arsenic, with a wild 'Ha! ha!'
findings.source_locator: rehearsal scene, after Hagar's incantation and before 'It's the best we've had yet'
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the chapter's most distinctively comic lines—'remorse and arsenic' is prosodically and tonally singular, establishing Alcott's ironic narrative register and introducing Jo as a melodrama-loving writer. Its absence erases a primary voice-signature moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full rehearsal passage: 'Don Pedro defied the world in a speech of two pages… Hugo died in agonies of remorse and arsenic, with a wild "Ha! ha!"'

findings.source_passage: "I don't see how you can write and act such splendid things, Jo. You're a regular Shakespeare!" exclaimed Beth
findings.source_locator: after the rehearsal, before Jo's Macbeth parody
findings.why_it_matters: Beth's 'regular Shakespeare' line and Jo's Macbeth parody ('Is that a dagger that I see before me?') are critical for establishing Jo's identity as an aspiring writer-actress; this is the first major signal of her literary ambition in the novel and is critically noted.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Beth's Shakespeare exclamation and Jo's modest reply, plus the Macbeth quotation and the toasting-fork punchline, as these are interpretive keystones for Jo's character arc.

findings.source_passage: "No, it's the toasting fork, with mother's shoe on it instead of the bread. Beth's stage-struck!" cried Meg, and the rehearsal ended in a general burst of laughter.
findings.why_it_matters: The punchline that closes the rehearsal is the comic payoff of the entire scene; without it, the scene's tonal arc is severed and the chapter loses a characteristic Alcott comic deflation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the toasting-fork punchline as the scene's closing beat.

findings.source_passage: she was not elegantly dressed, but a noble-looking woman… 'Well, dearies, how have you got on to-day? There was so much to do, getting the boxes ready to go to-morrow, that I didn't come home to dinner. Has any one called, Beth? How is your cold, Meg? Jo, you look tired to death. Come and kiss me, baby.'
findings.source_locator: Marmee's entrance, after actors and audience turn to welcome her
findings.why_it_matters: Marmee's specific maternal inquiries ('How is your cold, Meg? Jo, you look tired to death. Come and kiss me, baby') are voice-defining for her character and establish the warmth-register of the novel's domestic world; the draft replaces them with a vague paraphrase ('happy little inquiries').
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Marmee's spoken greeting verbatim or near-verbatim; the specific details ('tired to death,' 'Come and kiss me, baby') are character-establishing.

findings.source_passage: the mother was a born singer. The first sound in the morning was her voice, as she went about the house singing like a lark; and the last sound at night was the same cheery sound, for the girls never grew too old for that familiar lullaby.
findings.why_it_matters: The 'born singer' / 'singing like a lark' coda is the chapter's closing grace-note, establishing Marmee's musical presence as a motif running through the novel; the draft collapses it to 'their mother's voice… the same cheery lullaby,' losing the lark image and the 'born singer' characterization.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'the mother was a born singer… singing like a lark' and 'the girls never grew too old for that familiar lullaby' to preserve the chapter's closing cadence.

summary: The draft's most serious failure is the near-total erasure of the comic rehearsal sequence—including 'Hugo died in agonies of remorse and arsenic,' Beth's 'regular Shakespeare,' Jo's Macbeth parody, and the toasting-fork punchline—removing the chapter's primary signature comedy and the first major signal of Jo's literary ambition; secondary losses include Marmee's specific maternal greeting and the 'born singer / singing like a lark' closing motif.
